title: Pipes and redirection
description: Compose a command line from a command, a stdout destination and a stderr destination, and see where each stream and each file ends up.
intro: Start with the preset `Save the output` and notice that the error message still appears on the screen. Then pick `Everything in one file`, and switch the stderr choice to the `before` variant of `2>&1`: predict what changes before you look. Finally, send the output of `grep` through a pipe and count the lines.
takeaways: Every command has three streams: standard input (0, normally the keyboard), standard output (1) and standard error (2). Both output streams go to the terminal unless you redirect them.
`>` sends stdout to a file and empties the file first. `>>` appends to the end instead. `2>` and `2>>` do the same for stderr. `<` makes a file the stdin of the command.
`|` connects the stdout of the command on its left to the stdin of the command on its right. It carries only stdout: error messages still go to the terminal unless you also redirect them.
`2>&1` makes stderr go to the place where stdout points at that moment, so the order matters: `> out.txt 2>&1` puts both in the file, but `2>&1 > out.txt` leaves the errors on the screen.
`2> /dev/null` discards error messages. `wc -l < build.log` prints only the number, while `wc -l build.log` also prints the file name.

commands.label: ls nothere build.log
stderr: ls: cannot access 'nothere': No such file or directory
commands.explain: `ls` lists `build.log` on stdout and complains about the missing `nothere` on stderr.

commands.label: grep ERROR missing.log build.log
stderr: grep: missing.log: No such file or directory
commands.explain: `grep` prints the two `ERROR` lines of `build.log` on stdout, and an error for the file `missing.log` on stderr.

commands.label: wc -l build.log
commands.explain: `wc -l` given a file name counts its lines and prints the name after the number. It has nothing to say on stderr.

commands.label: wc -l < build.log
commands.explain: The shell opens `build.log` and connects it to stdin with `<`. `wc` never sees a file name, so it prints only the number.

presets.title: Save the output
presets.explain: `>` sends stdout to a file and empties the file first. The old line in `out.txt` is gone. The error is stderr, so it still shows on the screen.

presets.title: Keep adding to a log
presets.explain: `>>` appends, so the old line in `out.txt` stays and the new lines come after it. Errors still go to the screen.

presets.title: Hide the errors
presets.explain: `2>` redirects stream 2. Sending it to `/dev/null` throws the error messages away, and stdout still reaches the screen.

presets.title: Output and errors in separate files
presets.explain: Each stream has its own number: `>` is `1>` and `2>` is for errors. Neither file shows up on the screen.

presets.title: Everything in one file
presets.explain: Put `> out.txt` first, then `2>&1`: stderr is pointed at wherever stdout points now, so both streams go into `out.txt`.

presets.title: The order trap
presets.explain: With `2>&1` before `> out.txt`, stderr copies the screen first, and only afterwards stdout moves to the file. The error stays on the screen.

presets.title: Count the matches
presets.explain: `|` connects stdout of one command to stdin of the next. `wc -l` counts the lines it receives. The error is not part of stdout, so it is not counted.

presets.title: Count the errors too
presets.explain: `2>&1` puts stderr into the pipe with stdout, so `wc -l` counts the error line as well.

presets.title: Read a file with <
presets.explain: `<` connects a file to stdin. With a file name as an argument, `wc` prints the name too. With `<` it prints only the number.
